OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
10 questions about these letters. Each answer is shown with the people who held it; this page does not choose between them.
James the Lord's brother, a son of Joseph and Mary (the "Helvidian" view, after Helvidius, 4th century)
J. B. Mayor (1892), who examines all three theories of the Lord's brothers

The plain reading of Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55 names James as a brother of Jesus. Because the brothers did not believe in him during his ministry, they cannot have been among the Twelve; the risen Jesus appeared to James, and Paul calls him "the Lord's brother" and a "pillar" of the Jerusalem church. Mark 6:3 Matthew 13:55 John 7:5 1 Corinthians 15:7 Galatians 1:19 Galatians 2:9 [1]
The Lord's brother as a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage (the "Epiphanian" view, after Epiphanius, a 4th-century bishop)

Examined by Mayor; Bigg reports that Clement of Alexandria held it of Jude, following the tradition in the Protevangelium of James; Eusebius says only that James was called the Lord's brother as a son of Joseph
An early tradition that keeps the brothers as real family of Joseph's household while preserving Mary's virginity. Mark 6:3 [1][3][10]
A cousin, the same man as James the son of Alphaeus, one of the Twelve (the "Hieronymian" view, after Jerome)
Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men ch. 2; Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897)

"Brother" is read in the wider sense of kinsman: Jerome made James the son of a sister of the Lord's mother, which lets the writer be one of the apostles. Matthew 10:3 Acts 1:13 Galatians 1:19 [13][21]
Undecided between the son of Alphaeus and a Jerusalem leader
John Calvin (1551)

Calvin thought the "pillar" of Galatians 2:9 was more likely the apostle, the son of Alphaeus, because he doubted a non-apostle would rank above apostles — but he declined to say which James wrote the letter. Galatians 2:9 [8]
A later writer using the name, or a Jewish work lightly made Christian

Spitta (a Jewish treatise with "Jesus Christ" added at 1:1 and 2:1), as reported by the ISBE; Davidson, Hilgenfeld, Baur, Zeller, Hausrath, von Soden, Jülicher, Harnack and Bacon, who dated it between about 70 and 150
The letter has little explicit Christian teaching and is written in good Greek. James 1:1 James 2:1 [17]
